segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I appreciate you coming here as we start. Let me tell you why we are doing this—they go to school here. You know, they go to school here. They are going to, one day, listen to us talking this good Cherokee. I don’t know if they can get that far in speaking, but they are going to want to listen to good Cherokee speaking. And, another thing, if you have grandchildren, they might want to listen to you talking. They will let them hear you speak, if they come here.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: As we begin, tell me your full name in English.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Watie Glass.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What, in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Tsuwanosgi Vdagedi.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Tsuwanosgi Vdagedi, where were you born?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Tahlequah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: At that old --

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: -- What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: -- where that old place was.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Sally Bull Hollow they call it—past Bell. It’s on the other side. I don’t know if you know where it’s at?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I know where it’s at—Sally Bull’.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: That’s where I grew up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was it like growing up there, what could you do?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: It was really great. It was really good. It was about 1970 when I got out of there—out of that hollow. I got out. I really did get out. I never went back. I got out and found a job, I was lazy. [before that]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How many were in your family?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: There was just four of us—two of us kids. Yeah, a girl and me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Both of you spoke Cherokee?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we all spoke fluent Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What could y’all do, growing up there in Sally Bull’, where y’all lived?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What was there to do, when y’all lived in Sally Bull’?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: There was nothing we could do, there in Sally Bull’. But when we got out of there, we worked. My sister started working first. There was a bus running. She would get in there—she was working in Bentonville, she would get in there—they fixed chickens in Bentonville. She would get in there every morning. She would come back in the evening. And I was home. I wasn’t doing anything, you know. My dad started getting in there. My dad and the girl were getting in there, going to work. Me and Mom were home alone. Because I was lazy, I wasn’t doing anything. I was home, I was just eating. Mom would cook. When they would get back in the evening, it would be time to eat. It would be getting dark, sometimes, when they got back in the evenings. Especially when they changed time. [Shift work] They would get back at dark, they would eat, then it would be time to lay down. In just a little while they would get back up. They would get back in the bus again. When it became my time to work, I worked with chickens for a little while. I was catching chickens for a while—about two weeks. Then I did something else there, at the chicken factory. And then my work just became lighter. It got where I really liked it. I had a good job.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where did you go to school at?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I kinda went to school at Bell. I went to the sixth-grade. I didn’t know nothing, they didn’t teach me nothing. They put papers on my desk and told me to read. When I went in, first, they told me to read. I said, “I don’t know how to do anything. I can’t read.” Then I got a whipping for not reading. That’s what they were doing to me. Telling me to read.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t speak English when you started?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, I didn’t speak English. And what little English I do speak, I just picked it up here and there. From people talking, you know—just from people talking I picked up this English I’m talking. I didn’t speak English until then.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Where was it you said you worked?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Decatour, Decatour, Arkansas. I became friends with people—like the banker there in Decatour. But they are gone, they passed away.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How long did you work there?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: 40 years.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: 40 years.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Are you retired now?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, I have retired. Yeah, I am glad I am retired. I had heart surgery, you know. I had to quit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, it wasn’t ‘cause you wanted to?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, that doctor in ‘05 said, “You are going to have to quit.” I said, “Alright.” I first had back surgery. First, I had surgery on my back. I asked if I could work again. “If you want to work that much, I will let you.” He told me. After back surgery I went back to work. Yeah, he let me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It didn’t bother you, while you were working?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, I was able to work. But then I had a heart attack. You know, then he made me quit for good. “There ain’t no use you working,” he told me.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: “If someone else’s back did that, they would’ve quit then.”

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I didn’t want to quit working. I did take a break from it, until it healed up a little bit, then I started back.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you have kids?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No. Yeah, I have one boy. I have one boy—he works here at Cherokee Nation. I don’t know what he does, but he works doing something for Cherokee Nation.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does he speak Cherokee?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, but he won’t speak to me in Cherokee. But he does speak Cherokee. I’ll say anything in Cherokee. He will understand, but he won’t speak to me in Cherokee. He never speaks to me in Cherokee, but he does understand Cherokee. He did go to school, and finished high school.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So he finished, huh?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all have electricity?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: We didn’t have electricity.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about water-that-came-to-the-house?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, we didn’t have it. It wasn’t until that Mankiller got in, then we had water in the house. When Wilma got in.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you still live in Sally Bull’?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, at that time, yeah. We still lived in Sally Bull’—when she got in. [Wilma Mankiller]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you came out of Sally Bull’, where did you go?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I went right there, to Salem.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you didn’t move very far?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, I didn’t move very far.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you like it there?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yes, I like it there, now. I just live past the Salem cemetery. I can see the church, if I stand in the yard. If I stand in the yard, I can see the church.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It’s not where they call Preachers Lane, is it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Just past it, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When your dad was working at the chicken plant, was that y’all’s income?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah. His name was Lawrence, I remember.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, at Preachers Lane?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Steve and all of them worked there, that was Steve.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: With the chickens?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, Steve and Mike—I don’t know if you know Mike.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he pass away?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, he passed away.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I knew him.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: You knew him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, he was the youngest, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, he was the youngest boy.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Steve’s back hurts him pretty bad, too. And he still drives a truck now.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Does he still pastor at that church in Marble City?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Boy, I don’t know. Last week we were talking to his wife, I forgot to ask her that. He did pastor there, didn’t he? Yeah, he might still be the pastor there, I was thinking. He preaches at Salem, sometimes, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you all were growing up, did your dad have time to plant a garden?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, you could say he planted a garden.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did he do to plow the ground?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: My dad?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Well, he would use a garden tiller, sometimes. He had a garden tiller he would use, you know, sometimes. The One-that-lived-‘long-time-ago had horses—it had two things to plow—double shovel. He would use that to plow. He would make it good, just with a double shovel. And then he would plant there. He would make it good with just that. 'Long time ago they had horses that would plow. He would make it look pretty with that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were you small?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, I was little. I was lazy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When your dad was planting a garden, did your mom preserve that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, she preserved it and canned it. In the wintertime, we ate that—tomatoes and blackberries, different things. ‘Long time ago that’s what they did to blackberry. Nowadays you can’t save it. You know what happens to blackberry. Now it ruins real quick, because it’s too hot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When I find out it’s turning ripe, I start chasing it.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It really ruins quick.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: And bugs tear it up.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Me and Lawrence used to look for blackberries all the time. It just falls apart now, that blackberry.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He probably planted potatoes.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What did he do to preserve them?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: We dug them out, or he dug them out. I used to help him dig them out, and we would clean them. He would just put them underneath, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: The house?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, he would just put them under the house. And when he wanted, he would go get enough of them for us to eat—you know, he would fix them, and it would work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they make it through the winter?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, they made it through the winter. He had it fixed good, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: He probably gave things away, too.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: There was a house there. But, them boys that used to live there, or they still around there, burned down that house. It was an old house. They burned it. He had a smoke house for meat—hog meat. We had hogs. They were fat. He would kill them himself. He would kill two, and save the meat. Boy, we would be eating hog meat.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did somebody help him?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah. Me, I was big enough, then, to help him.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, the laziness had passed.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, I used to help him ‘cause I wanted to eat it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It really is hard work—especially if you kill two.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s hard work. It ain’t easy, it’s hard work.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: When you get done fixing one, you are going to sleep from getting tired.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They didn’t throw nothing away, did they?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They used it all.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They used all of it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all fix those intestines?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, my mom would fix them. I’ll say. Boy, they were good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you liked them.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: She mixed in a little hot pepper. They were the same as the hot links they have there in Stilwell. [Spicy smoked sausage] They were delicious. Some don’t like hot links, but I like those hot links. You know, boy—those homemade hot links they make are delicious.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you liked them?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, I really liked them. They make some good things, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about corn, when they make hominy?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they make that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah. Hominy, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You didn’t learn how they did that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, I didn’t, not that. I know they put that in kvnvtsi. [Cherokee hickory nut dish] What it was, hominy. When they would brew kvnvtsi, they would put it in there. It was delicious, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Which one do you like better, that, or what they call rice? [Kvnvtsi, hickory nut dish, rice and hominy (maize, corn) can be added]

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I like them both. It don’t matter. No, it don’t matter. I would drink, eat them both. Rice is delicious, too. I wouldn’t not want it. I’ll drink it, also. [Kvnvtsi is a broth-like liquid] ‘Really good if you put rice in it, too, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about things from the woods, did y’all use that? Like squirrels.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, squirrels and rabbits, we killed them. George Livers, do you know him? Me and him would go and look for squirrels. We would kill lots of squirrels, and Dad would clean all of those. He would sit down and clean them all. And when he cleaned them all, Mom would cook them. The next day, boy, we would eat some delicious squirrels.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did she preserve some?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, some. Not a lot. Just a few, you know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That gravy was good, ain’t it? Made from that squirrel.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that rabbit gravy was delicious, too.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I would prefer that than squirrel.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, rabbit, ain’t it. Yeah. They would pour that gravy on top of that rabbit. When they had fried rabbit, they would pour it on there. Boy, it was good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I’m hungry now.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I don’t know why. I guess we were just hungry back then. I think we were really hungry, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Or we were dependent on that, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we were eating extremely good back then, ain’t it. We was, extremely.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We just didn’t know we were poor, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, but we weren’t really poor of anything... Though, was we? And we weren’t starving.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, we weren’t starving. We had clothes on.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: We had clothes on. We wasn’t hungry. We weren’t naked. No, we weren’t naked, Charlie. Also, we had clothes to wear, ain’t it? The Whites did us poorly.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the way they looked at us—like poor people. They looked at us like that. But, as far as we know, we wasn’t in poor condition, if we was poor. What about onion and poke salad, did your mom preserve that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: She didn’t preserve it. We were eating it. We were eating it as fast as she could pull it, we pulled. And poke salad, too. You know, we really didn’t like it preserved. We ate it, just the same. We thought eating it one time was enough—in the summertime. If it was preserved it broke up. It’s good though, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s good.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: If you put egg in it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about mustard greens?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Mustard greens. Yeah, it’s good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Have you ever ate it with egg put in it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, with eggs mixed in it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, it was really good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Me, last night, I got fed onion, mustard greens, and watercress, and beans.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: And beans, boy.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And fry bread.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: You ate good.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, I ate good. What about mushrooms?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: If you can find them, you can cook them. My neighbor looks for them. If he finds some, he brings them. They might stick on, I was thinking, now that we got a little rain. I heard a while ago that it’s supposed to rain sometime this week.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you also like those unisqula, morels?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Those are what they call ‘morels’.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My wife preserves those.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Is that right?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: She cuts them small, and soaks them in water. And soaks them in water for a little while, then she puts them in a freezer bag.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: She preserves them, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They are good to eat.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: That girl-that-lives-by-the-house, she seems to always find them. [Fungi] She finds them all the time. She walks around a lot. And she just sells them. You know, she don’t eat them. She just sells them. She would take them to Vonnie Jones and sell them, she said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you think, sometimes, what do you remember the most?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: When I lived in Sally Bull’, are you saying, the most?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, what do you think of, the most, growing up there?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Uh let’s see. Well, when I think about it, I think about growing up real good. I think about it, there. When I think—me and the boys—we carried on and played around with them-that-lived-there-then. We didn’t drink, and we didn’t smoke that stuff, and use that dope—that, we didn’t use that. That changed, all of a sudden. You know that happened, you know. I still don’t do that. I have never done that. I was afraid to do that. But, them other boys did that pretty quick. We used to live good, you know? It was a good place to stay. It was a good place to live. Real quick, it was good to live there. It was quiet.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did y’all visit each other?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, at nighttime we would walk.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Nobody had a car.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, we walked. I don’t know if you know Franklin Sawney?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They would come straight off the mountain. Him and his brother Jody. They carried a kerosene lantern. They would be shining the light. They would come straight off and come to our house and visit us. They would stay a long time. Then, at night, they would light it back up, and go back up. They would come over and just be talking. They didn’t play any games, they just talked.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would just talk.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Talked about hunting, and looking for squirrels, and hunting rabbits.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about you kids? Did they let you listen to their conversations?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Not really. Some of it. But, as for me, they never chased me away.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They didn’t.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, but the others did get chased off. You know. But, as for me, I never got chased off—I would listen to them talking.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did you like it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, I could listen, though. They wouldn’t chase me off. But them others would get chased off.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They didn’t slow down doing anything. That’s what was against them. [The kids] When they would get chased off. If it wasn’t for that, they might have just sat there. But they didn’t slow down, yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about when y’all got sick, did you go to the doctor or...?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I didn’t know what a doctor was back then. We just used medicine from the woods. You know, something you brewed. Different things, my mom knew how. It would’ve been good if I knew. But I have forgotten it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Alitsi Vdagedi, and my mom was Celi Vdagedi—my parents.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was it Linch, in English? What was it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Richard Glass—his brother was Linch Glass—Alitsi, yeah. He’s not alive, that Linch Glass. He died. And George Glass.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s the one that lived towards Greasy.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, they called him Udasvdi. He died, too.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He’s been dead a long time, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: He lived towards Greasy for a long time, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Keyogi was his wife’s name.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you remember some of that medicine your mom used?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Boy, that would really help, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: That hickory bark—four pieces of bark, you boil and drink it. They say it will help you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What with?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Hickory bark.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What will it help you with?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Just anything in your body that’s happening, making you sick. They say it will help you.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So y’all just used things like that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, just things like that. And it grows around the water, at my house. Oh—you don’t know where I live—by the church. There is lots of those plants. That-Girl was telling me the name of it, but I forgot its name. If you break it, it will make a sound. It will break easy if you do this [gestures] it will make a sound. It smells really good to me. Some people don’t like it, but it smells good. And he said, “If you cut about six of them. And that hickory bark,” he said. “If you put them together, and tie them together. And soak them. And let them boil. And let it make a soup, good. And drink it while it’s still warm.” He said, “That will help you the best, and clean you out if you’re sick.” There is some close to the house. I wanted to get some off, just here, pretty soon. You know it’s in the clearing by the house. You don’t even have to walk in the grass.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So you haven’t tried it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I haven’t tried it, yet. ‘Long time ago when I was just a child I did try it. It has helped me. As far as I know it helped me, extremely. As far as I know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you didn’t hardly go to the doctor?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, I hadn’t been to the doctor ‘till I grew up. I didn’t know what the doctor... I really didn’t, I didn’t know what the doctor was like.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: When I grew up, then I went to the doctor.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you moved from there, which is Bell. Or, when you were growing up, they used to play baseball. Did you play?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, I never did. Did you?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, a little bit.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: You played a little bit.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, they were already quitting. It wasn’t that much anymore.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, at Greasy? They had a big ball field, ain’t it? Who was your sister? [Dianna]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Marie is her name.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Marie.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Is she still alive?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Do you remember Rainwater Kimble?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s her dad, this-One.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Is that your dad? [Dianna]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: That was his wife that passed away. [Clara Kimble]

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, boy that Rainwater Kimble is a nice person, ain’t it? That’s your dad?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: The one that passed away that’s your mom?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Y’all look alike. That’s why I asked you who you was.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That’s how you recognized me.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, y’all look alike.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You are talking about her mom. You are really talking bad about her mom.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s why I asked you. That’s who I thought it was, a while ago. I thought she passed away. And she came here. It was you that came. Is that old man still alive?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, he’s still alive. Tonight I’m going back that way. I spend the night with him sometimes. He’s crippled now.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: He’s crippled?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yeah, just a little—he pushes one of those things around.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Boy, I fell down Friday. I didn’t get up till Saturday morning, when That-Boy helped me up. Friday, all day, and Friday night. It was Saturday morning when he helped me up. I fell down real quick. I don’t know what happened. It was inside the house. Boy, I couldn’t get up. And this morning, again, I almost fell down. I don’t know the reason. They gave me a shot of [vitamin] B12. [They said] I think they are lying, and didn’t give me a shot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They give me a shot, too. And I’m thinking the same thing—it don’t seem like it’s helping me with anything.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me too. I give myself shots every week. It seems like it don’t help me either.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: It didn’t even hurt when they gave me a shot. It would hurt more if a wasper stung me. That didn’t even hurt.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: “You are going to have more energy,” they tell me. I haven’t found more energy.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Boy, I don’t know. They said I couldn’t go in there. I got to have that ‘security guard’ if I go in there, anywhere—for six months, they told me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Why is that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I get on to them nurses, they told me.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh...

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huh...

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I don’t know why. I wasn’t doing that to them. But them nurses said that a letter came to the house, saying that—telling me that. I can’t go in without that ‘security guard’, it said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh...

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: But, I don’t care. You know? I’m going to make that ‘security guard’ do everything, when I get there. He’s got to do everything—that’s what that paper says. [Letter]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh. That’s the first time I heard that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me, too.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I thought “Do they know that here, too?” When the ‘security guard’ followed me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really, security guard.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, he drove my pickup. He brought me here. And he drove it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Hmm...

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: ‘While ago, the first time me and the ‘security guard’ were together.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh...

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I don’t know why, either.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I don’t know either.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They think you are really mean.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They think I am mean. I asked them, “I wasn’t saying nothing to them nurses.” They got mad at me about something, I guess.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They should be doing more of them like that. ‘Cause I’ve heard of them getting on to them.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, they get on to them. Yeah, and just asked them to get my pills ready. I didn’t cuss, or cuss at them. The head nurse—the main, main nurse, we had a talk. I said “Let me tell you, they don’t have to do this for me.” I told her. “It’s like they feel like they have to do this for me,” I told her. “I don’t care. They don’t have to do this for me. I know that ain’t their job.” I told her. “I don’t want to give them another job. I don’t have to take them pills.” I told her. “You tell them that, too.” I guess she told them, real quick. They were calling me. They wouldn’t stop calling me. “Bring him in. We will fix them pills.” They were saying.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They got on to you.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They didn’t?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, they were in a hurry to fill them pills. They filled them up, and now I have them all full.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was you at that Mankiller? [Wilma P. Mankiller Health Center, Stilwell]

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah Mankiller. That’s their job—the doctor said it was OK.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They do my dad like that, too, sometimes. They forget to fill his pills. And when we get them, we put them in that thing he has. They will forget to fill one. [The nurses]

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They will just do whatever—if you let it go.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: When you were growing up --

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: -- What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: -- When you were growing up, what was the most important thing, to you, that your parents taught you?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They tried extremely hard so that I could get an education. They encouraged me extremely hard. For me to learn. But it never happened. Like I said, that’s what happened when I got school—they would throw the papers where I was sitting, and tell me to read. I can’t read. I don’t know how to do anything. You know it would have been good, if they were teaching me. If they were teaching me, it would’ve been different, you know. But they weren’t teaching me, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, they just laid them on there.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, they just laid them on there. They just laid them on there. Just like them papers you have. If you told me to read them, I can’t read them, you know. That’s just what they did to me, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They didn’t scold you for talking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, they didn’t scold me for talking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, they just wanted you to learn?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, nobody has ever scolded me for talking Cherokee. I’ll tell them, if they scold me for talking Cherokee, you know, they will be saying something they shouldn’t say.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about the cook stove, did y’all use a wood burner?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, all wood burner. Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Which would you prefer now? Cooking with wood, or what they have now?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: The wood burner. If you use a wood burner, you’d say it’s good. It’s really good. I don’t know why there is a difference between wood burner [and gas or electrical cooking].

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There is a difference, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, there is a difference. I guess ‘cause things cook slow—if it’s gas or electric, it cooks real quick.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Real quick. Boy, those beans, ain’t it—cooked with, using wood.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, cooked with, using wood, it’s good. Man, that’s beyond measure. Brown beans, ain’t it? Yeah they are really good. You wouldn’t never get enough of that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Was there a water creek close to your house, growing up?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, there was a creek close by, and there was a spring just above.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s what I hear from all the people I talk to. They make it clear that they lived close to water.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we lived close to water.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about the house? How big of a house did y’all live in?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Ah, let’s see, about three bedrooms was the size of the house we lived in.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So it was that big—the house that y’all lived in?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we did that ourselves. When it started, it was just the kitchen and living room.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Just me and Dad added on rooms, you know. With boards we just got from the lumber yard. We just made rooms. We made it to three bedrooms, just doing it ourselves. It was a pretty good house. It was warm. It was warm. We lived there a long time. We didn’t freeze. We never did freeze, you know, we were warm.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: And y’all just burned wood.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: We had a fireplace. Boy, that fireplace was beautiful.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did your dad build it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, it was already there. But Dad did fix it up. He fixed it good. Boy, dawatsili this long [gestures]. Dawatsili wood about this big [gestures]. We would go get them, somewhere over this way, towards where the Bell community building is. Somewhere over towards the edge of a field. Dawatsili this big [gestures]. They were old. He had a little truck, and put them on there. We would take them at night. So, he could put them in the fire at night. He said they would last all night. He would put them in there. Boy the flames would be beautiful. Boy, it would be shining bright. Man, there would be a hot fire. It would be hot in there—from the fire in the fireplace, you know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That flame is beautiful, ain’t it? I have a big fireplace at my house. Sometimes we use it just so we can watch it.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: It’s beautiful, yeah. In that old house you couldn’t see even a little bit of cold. It would be warm in there, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I guess they were all like that, ain’t it? Them elders, ‘cause my dad would have a warm, hot fire.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: You know, those houses with the spaces between the boards for air to come in—if you burn wood, that will take care of the spaces. You can’t feel those, it will cover the house. [Keep all of it warm]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh...

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: It will let warm in. You can’t even tell there are spaces. It will let warm air in the house. That’s how good that wood is to burn. That woodstove I have sitting at the house. That’s the only one I have. If I light that, boy, there will be warm air everywhere—that’s a good one.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is that all y’all used, was that fireplace, or, did y’all have another stove?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we had a stove. We used gas, and we also had a wood stove, too. You know I don’t hardly use it. [gas] I build a fire, sometimes. I should be building a fire all the time.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That, what they call—dogwood.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Do you know the name in Cherokee? Dogwood, let me see. Boy, I sure don’t know its name.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Those—when they get old—they burn good, too.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Dogwood.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Gitli vdi I guess?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They called it something, but I forget.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Let me ask you this—lots don’t believe this, what they call ‘Bigfoot’, what do you think about that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They say they have seen it. But I don’t know if it’s true.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did they see it at Bell?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: That’s what they say, somewhere.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I’ll tell you—I can’t tell anyone ‘cause I was by myself—I’m just telling you two. I’m not lying to y’all. I have seen something like that. But it wasn’t just out towards Bell. It was when I was working. I was driving a truck, it was in the evening. I was driving a truck. I left from Decatour. I was pulling a chicken loader. I went around a curve, towards this way, it came out running fast. It was about this tall [gestures] in the grass. It popped out, just its head was sticking out. I seen a scary-looking man. I don’t know if it was that ‘Bigfoot’. They say they had been seeing it around there. I heard, I thought, that must be that Bigfoot—I seen it. It was something amazing—an ugly person I seen, it had hair all over his face.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: How tall would you say it was?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Probably about five foot.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Oh, so he wasn’t tall?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, he was about that tall. [Five feet]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did he cross the road?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, he didn’t. He stood a little ways away. I drove by and looked, and he stood just over there. He popped out, I seen him. I was driving in a truck—he didn’t cross the road. I don’t know if it was human, but it was something. If it would’ve crossed, I would know more. But, like I said, that’s just what I know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They talk about it out towards Belfonte, too.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That they have also seen it.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: That they have seen it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: There, too.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They looked for it. Lots of people came to CC Camp. [Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) camp]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Where them Cochrans have that place. There were a lot gathered there, and they looked for it. They didn’t find nothing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Huh...

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, they looked for it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Just there, close by in the woods? They looked for it.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They drove their cars. They looked for it all day. Yeah, like Thomas, and different ones, looked for it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They didn’t find nothing?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, they didn’t find nothing.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about what us natives believe, in our words ‘booger man’ they call them. Have you ever seen anything strange like that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You haven’t.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I haven’t.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about have you heard anyone talking about it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: I’ve heard about it, though.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they talking about something scary?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Were they talking about something scary?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They were just talking about seeing a ‘booger man’, you know.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about little people. Do you believe that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Little people, do you believe that, they call them?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Little people?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, I have heard them.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: So, you have heard them?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, they come by my house almost all the time. They come by, close to them houses. You know, they will come by. They will be talking, I can hear them talking.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They haven’t ever come to your house?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, ‘never have. This morning, I don’t know who it was, I will tell you right now. This morning, something made a sound when I looked at the wall. ‘Didn’t have a mirror. Right here someone was peeking at me, just about here [gestures]. But, from here, I couldn’t see. I could just see it, right here. And, like they wear at the hospital, they have on so they can breathe that oxygen—that’s what it had on, in both its nostrils. And it had that tube here. It was looking at me, and I was looking at it. I couldn’t never tell who it was, for a long time, about 30 minutes I looked at it. I just looked the other way. I never could tell who it was looking at it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: It stayed like that for that long?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, I guess, when I looked away, it faded away. It was about four o’clock in the morning. In the glass by the door, it was like that. I don’t know what it was, but that is the first time I have ever seen anyone doing that. I guess it was a ‘booger man.’

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They call them ‘shape-shifters.’

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, shape-shifters. It didn’t even scare me a little bit. I got a good look at it. But I don’t know who it was. I hope it comes to see me again, later.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Maybe you can have a talk with it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, we will have a talk.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Did your dad ever have any fox-chasing dogs?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, and Dalosi—did you know him?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah, is he a Livers, yeah. [Livers family]

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, George’s dad. Yeah we lived close by. Where I was telling you—in Sally Bull’. We lived close by. And you know that cow horn, he had one. And, when George’s dad and my dad wanted to go hunting, he would blow that cow horn. He would blow it, two or three times, then he would listen. And Dalosi would blow his cow horn. Then they would meet, somewhere in the middle. They would have dogs, then go hunting. That’s what they would do to call each other, you know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: My grandpa had one like that. He used to do that. Snow Gonzales—I don’t know if you know him?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, they would hunt all night. Even now it’s still at the house, what Dad used. That-Boy has it there. My dad said, when we would build a fire when we were cold, Dalosi would not even put a wood in the fire. He would be standing there getting warm, he said. He wouldn’t even put a wood in the fire. [Dad] would have to do it all, he said.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: My dad used to do that, too. He had dogs. I don’t know if you knew him? They called him Tsigili, Lee Bunch.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Was Tsigili your dad?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: No, he [Dad] hunted with him.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Yeah, I knew him. [Tsigili, Lee Bunch]

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They would all go, all night.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: All night, huh?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: What about, have you ever heard about anything about the Cherokees being driven here? Or if your parents or your grandmother or your grandfather was a part of that?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: No, not that.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: You haven’t?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: ‘Never have.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: We are going to finish now. But I’m asking this last—how we are talking, this Cherokee, what’s going to happen to it?

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: What’s going to happen?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: How we are talking Cherokee—it won’t fall apart as far as I know. It going to make good progress, I believe. If those children don’t forget it. If those children forget it, ’is the only way it’s going to go away. That’s the only way it’s going away—if the children don’t want to talk it.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: I appreciate you for coming, we are finished.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: OK. What do you think?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: Well, this school here. They are not learning like we are talking.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: They’re not.

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They talk a little different. I think it will live on, but it won’t be the way we are talking. It’s a little broken, the way they will be talking. It won’t be as good as we are talking now. They won’t be able to talk like that. If a student from here is talking to me, I have to listen good, to understand what they are saying. They put it a little different now. I don’t know, I don’t think it will be the way we are talking.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Just like Spanish, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: They say it’s easier to learn Spanish than it is to learn Cherokee. Might be best if we just learn Spanish.

segments.speaker: watie-glass
segments.translation: Who wanted it to be that terrible?

segments.speaker: charlie-shell
segments.translation: That’s just the way they are teaching, or learning. I don’t know which. I don’t know why they speak that way. Cherokee will be here, but it will not be the way we are talking, ‘is the way that I think about it.
